rv.q: There is merriment in the confusion and its untangling, but also a dream-like instability in a punchy, satisfying show.

Simplicity itself, but all you need when you have this glorious play, well performed. The admirable David Birrell as Feste the fool, and the three excellent musicians Hazel Monaghan, Nicholas Hann and Evie Hilyer-Ziegler bookend the show with ethereal music by Genevieve Dawson which sets the scene and finally promises to ‘please us every day’.
Glover’s Twelfth Night is an enjoyable production whose strongest moments demonstrate the possibilities of physical comedy and inventive stagecraft.
Painlessly cut and played at a cracking pace, this production validates Twelfth Night ‘s position as the finest of Shakespeare’s comedies.
Jamie Glover’s production has moments of magical promise
This is Shakespeare at his slick, witty and energetic best, the dialogue fizzing along and the actors carrying the story (and the audience) along with ease.
Great acting, and a magnificent comedy.
This is a hugely entertaining production and showcases the talent and versatility of this fine company of actors.
Jamie Glover's Twelfth Night has a great pace to it, with the humour of the second act driving a glorious and vibrant evening.
It’s a production that oozes energy and flair.
Glover brings energy and clarity to the language.
Jordan stole the stage every time and he was one of the highlights of the show for me.

This production of Twelfth Night from Sheffield Theatres is brilliantly funny, and director Jamie Glover and his team have led the company to a product that is accessible, and full of energy and interesting character nuance.
Whilst it’s not a particularly creative production, it will give you a few laughs on these dark autumnal evenings.
My five stars aren't just for a fantastic production of Twelfth Night .
Overall, Twelfth Night at the Crucible Theatre is amusing Shakespeare.

cn.t: Critics praise this crowd-pleasing Twelfth Night for its physical comedy and strong performances, particularly Mathew Horne's Malvolio. While generally well-received as accessible Shakespeare, some find it falls short of being a standout hit.
